questions.question: ResNet architectures can successfully train networks with over 100 or even 1000 layers.
questions.explanation: True. ResNet solved the degradation problem, allowing training of networks with 100+ layers.

questions.question: The 'degradation problem' refers to the fact that adding more layers to a very deep network can lead to higher training error, even without overfitting.
questions.explanation: True. Degradation causes error rates to rise across both training and testing splits, pointing to optimization difficulties.

questions.question: ResNet identity mappings (shortcuts) contain a large number of learnable parameters.
questions.explanation: False. Skip connections contain no learnable parameters; they simply pass identity forward.

questions.question: What happens to the gradient during backpropagation in a very deep network without skip connections?
options: It becomes extremely small, preventing the early layers from learning.
It remains constant across all layers.
It only affects the Dropout layers.
questions.explanation: Without skip connections, gradients vanish in deep networks, preventing early layers from learning effectively.

questions.question: Data augmentation increases the size of your dataset on disk by saving thousands of new modified image files before training begins.
questions.explanation: False. Data augmentation generates transformations on-the-fly during training, not by saving new files.

questions.question: One of the key insights of VGGNet is that a stack of two 3x3 filters has the same effective receptive field as one 5x5 filter.
questions.explanation: True. Two 3x3 filters stacked achieve a 5x5 receptive field with fewer parameters.

questions.question: LeNet-5 utilized 5x5 convolutional filters.
questions.explanation: True. LeNet-5 used 5x5 filters in its convolutional layers.

questions.question: What is the defining architectural characteristic of VGGNet?
options: Using very large kernels (11x11) to capture more context.
Using small (3x3) filters exclusively and increasing depth.
The introduction of inception modules with parallel paths.
Eliminating the use of Max Pooling.
questions.explanation: VGGNet uses uniform 3x3 filters stacked in homogeneous blocks, increasing depth.

questions.question: What problem do 'Skip Connections' (or Identity Shortcuts) in ResNet primarily solve?
options: Vanishing gradients in very deep networks
Excessive memory usage from large kernels
questions.explanation: Skip connections allow gradients to flow directly through the network, solving the vanishing gradient problem.

questions.question: AlexNet was significantly deeper than LeNet-5, featuring 8 weight layers.
questions.explanation: True. AlexNet had 8 weight layers, making it much deeper than LeNet-5.

questions.question: LeNet-5 was famously designed for which specific application in the late 1990s?
questions.explanation: LeNet-5 was designed for handwritten digit recognition on MNIST in the late 1990s.

questions.question: When fine-tuning a pre-trained model, what kind of learning rate is typically recommended?
options: A very high learning rate to force rapid change.
A very low learning rate to make small, incremental adjustments.
The same learning rate used to train the original model.
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning uses a very low learning rate to make subtle adjustments without destroying pre-trained weights.

questions.question: If a system is invariant, a shift in the input leads to a corresponding shift in the output.
questions.explanation: False. Invariance means the output is unchanged despite input shifts. Equivariance means output shifts with input.

questions.question: Which operation in a CNN is primarily responsible for 'Equivariance', where the feature map shifts in tandem with the input?
questions.explanation: Convolution is equivariant: shifting input causes a corresponding shift in the output feature map.

questions.question: AlexNet won the ILSVRC 2012 competition by a very small margin (less than 1% error difference).
questions.explanation: False. AlexNet won by a monumental margin, significantly outperforming all other entries.

questions.question: What distinguishes Semantic Segmentation from Object Detection?
options: It only identifies the single most prominent object in the image.
It uses bounding boxes to wrap around objects.
It classifies every individual pixel in the image into a category.
It only works on grayscale images.
questions.explanation: Semantic Segmentation provides pixel-wise classification masks, unlike detection with bounding boxes.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of Data Augmentation used to prevent overfitting?
options: Horizontal flipping, rotation, and zooming of training images
Adding more neurons to the final dense layer
questions.explanation: Horizontal flipping, rotation, and zooming are common data augmentation techniques that increase data diversity.

questions.question: What is ImageNet in the context of Deep Learning?
options: A specific type of CNN architecture used for edge detection.
A massive dataset of over 14 million labeled images used for benchmarking.
A software library for data augmentation.
The name of the GPU used to train AlexNet.
questions.explanation: ImageNet is a large-scale dataset with millions of labeled images used for benchmarking computer vision models.

questions.question: Which computer vision task involves both identifying what objects are in an image and where they are located by drawing bounding boxes?
questions.explanation: Object Detection identifies objects with bounding boxes, combining classification and localization.

questions.question: AlexNet was originally trained across two GPUs because of the memory limitations of the time.
questions.explanation: True. AlexNet was split across two GPUs due to memory constraints in 2012.
